Volvo EX60 Manufacturing Difficulties Hinder Production Output, US Dealers Hit Worst
14 photos
Photo: Volvo
Volvo's most important electric vehicle yet is running at roughly a tenth of its planned output. As per a source cited by Automotive News, the EX60 line in Torslanda is building just around 10 percent of the 2,000 crossovers a week Volvo initially targeted, leaving the US dealership network without significant volume until deep into 2027.
About 500 units were delivered worldwide in July 2026, while August 2026 saw an estimated 250 deliveries. Volvo told its US-based dealers to plan for approximately 7,000 sales in 2027 alone, a figure that has recently morphed from a target to wishful thinking. Series production of the EX60 kicked off in the latter part of April 2026, meaning that the EX60 line has had about half a year to find its rhythm.
The weekly target of 2,000 units would have meant in the ballpark of 8,000 units per month, but alas, the summer tally ran to hundreds instead of thousands. Rather than the vehicle per se, manufacturing difficulties hindered the EX60's rollout. According to the insider cited by Automotive News, the problems concern the cell-to-body integration and the megacasting process.
Both have proven more complex to scale than originally assumed, and Volvo's paper trail is pretty blunt. In a memo sent to US dealers, the Swedish manufacturer acknowledges that introducing a brand-new platform and model into a running factory is always a challenge. That memo was sent to US retailers in September 2026.
In it, Volvo highlights that the delays are not related to product performance, safety, or quality. All in all, it's easy to understand why the ramp-up phase hasn't unfolded as expected. The company is presently prioritizing European markets, where electric vehicle adoption is much stronger than in the United States and Canada.
What that means is limited availability in North America into 2027, but a significant number of already allocated vehicles are certain to reach American retailers early next year. Shipments are expected to go back to normal in the second half of 2027. For dealers, Volvo is leaving a bunch of potential sales on the table while other legacy brands arrive with brand-new EVs of their own.
Photo: Volvo This wouldn't be the first time a Volvo electric model's rollout was hindered by problems. Remember the EX90? It launched much later than anticipated due to quality concerns, missing features, and software glitches, an experience that left many retailers wary of a repeat. Who could blame them? After all, the production-related issues of the more affordable EX60 proved them right.
Competing in the largest premium segment, the EX60 anchors the Swedish automaker's target of 200,000 annual US retail sales by 2030. This number looks increasingly distant with each compromised launch, especially after Volvo posted an 11 percent nosedive in global deliveries in the past quarter. China dropped the hardest, with Volvo noting a drop of 41 percent. US volume, on the other hand, slid a more manageable 8.7 percent.
Volvo has understandably scrapped its 2026 cash flow outlook, with Volvo also freezing white-collar hiring globally while also tightening outside spending. Meanwhile, the XC60 and the XC90 both delivered year-over-year growth in the US market in the third quarter of 2026.
Their plug-in hybrid versions deliver up to 78 and 73 miles of electric range, respectively, meaning 126 and 117 kilometers in metric speak. Both Mercedes and BMW are already shipping similarly sized premium electric crossovers, making the EX60's delay all the more unkind to dealers nationwide.
Before this stumble, chief exec Hakan Samuelsson projected about 60,000 global sales for the EX60 this year alone. With the EX60 assembly line running at a tenth of the projected weekly output, first-year production numbers will be truly disappointing. On the upside, kudos to Volvo for sorting things out instead of passing potential problems onto consumers.

BYD will launch the updated Seagull next week, its popular EV that sells for around $10,000 in China.
When is BYD launching the updated Seagull EV?
The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car in its home market. In China, the electric hatch starts at just 69,900 yuan, or roughly $10,000.
BYD sells the electric hatch in Europe and the UK as the Dolphin Surf. Elsewhere, it’s rebadged and sold as the Dolphin Mini.
Outside of China, the Dolphin Surf is among BYD’s lowest-priced EVs, starting at €22,900 ($25,000) in Europe.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
It’s no wonder the Seagull, including the Dolphin Surf and Mini, is one of the world’s top-selling EVs. According to the most recent data from Cleantechnica , BYD’s Seagull (Dolphin Surf/Mini) was the sixth most popular electric car in the world through the first eight months of 2026.
With a flood of low-cost competition arriving, BYD is preparing to launch an updated Seagull in China that will be bigger, smarter, and feel more premium.
BYD second-generation Seagull EV (Source: Zhang Zhuo)
According to a report from Chinese tech outlet IT Home News , BYD sent out a media invitation, confirming the second-generation Seagull will launch on October 20 at the Zhengzhou International Circuit.
The updated Seagull is bringing several major improvements. For one, it will be 425 mm longer, with a 150 mm longer wheelbase than the current Seagull.
A regulatory filing from China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) revealed the second-generation Seagull is 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase.
It also gains another seat, with room for five passengers. The updated version will use a more powerful 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) the current Seagull offers.
Unlike the current front-wheel-drive (FWD) Seagull, the second-generation model will switch to rear-wheel drive (RWD).
BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system to improve ride quality and handling.
The new Seagull will be available with two BYD lithium iron phosphate (LFP) Blade Batteries, offering CLTC ranges of up to 320 km and 420 km. Meanwhile, higher-priced trims will include BYD’s 1,500 kW Flash Charging technology.
This setup enables the battery to charge from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes just 9 minutes. Even at temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes 12 minutes to charge from 20% to 97%.
Inside, the interior is revamped with a larger center infotainment screen, a two-spoke steering wheel, a redesigned center console, and added physical buttons.
Like many of its new vehicles, the second-generation Seagull will receive updated safety and convenience features.
All models will have BYD’s 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system. Higher-priced variants will offer BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system and the DiPilot 300 driver assistance system with a roof-mounted LiDAR.
Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD’s Ocean series, announced that blind pre-orders for the updated Seagull opened on October 9. However, he didn’t disclose a price.
BYD will reveal prices during the launch event on October 20, but online rumors suggest dealers will “pre-deduct prices” for the second-generation Seagull at around 85,000 yuan, or about $12,500.
After it launches in China, BYD is expected to introduce the larger, upgraded model overseas. It will likely be some variation of the Dolphin Surf and Mini.

1993 Chevy C1500 Looks Almost Stock, but What's Under the Hood Changes Everything
24 photos
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube
This 1993 Chevrolet C1500 454 SS could have ended up in the crusher or be rotting in a backyard somewhere. However, life took a turn for the better for the good, old Chevy. Now, it rocks the streets, looking like the perfect sleeper, but roaring out all the drama of the big-block V8, which throws over 700 horsepower to the ground.
The man who is to blame for the build is Diego of Diego Creations. He bought a1993 Chevy C1500 454 SS Old Body Style (OBS), which was almost entirely stock at the time, and converted it into a street monster. The truck had the original big-block engine under the hood, but it had been bored out to 496. That changed along the way, but the exterior remained the same, as Diego wanted to keep the patina.
When General Motors initially launched the C1500 454 SS in 1990, it was offered exclusively in Onyx Black over a Garnet Red interior. In 1992 and 1993, GM expanded the lineup to include Summit White and Victory Red.
Because 1993 was the final and lowest-production year for the 454 SS, finding a factory-original Summit White truck with the original red interior makes it exceptionally rare, with production estimates tracking right around 65 units ever built in that specific combination.
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube This 1993 Chevrolet C1500 454 SS is one of the 65 built that year with a rare color combination: Summit White over a red interior. It was the rarity that convinced Diego to keep the interior and exterior as stock as possible. To lock in the surviving factory paint, Diego covered it with a Poppy's Patina clear coat.
Underneath, though, it is a whole different truck. It all starts with the LS3 416-cubic-inch V8 stroker engine, which has been fully built, still featuring the stock heads, but ported and polished, and sporting a modified crankshaft, forged H-beam connecting rods, and forged high-compression pistons.
The stock LSA blower with a Harrop lid kept its ground. The setup makes 715 horsepower to the wheels, which means around 900 horsepower at the crank. That is light-years away from the factory rating of the Chevy C1500 454 SS from back in the 1990s.
The truck rolled off the production line of the General Motors Fort Wayne Assembly Plant in Fort Wayne, Indiana, with the 454-cubic-inch (7.4-liter) big-block V8, which produced 255 horsepower (259 metric horsepower) and 405 pound-feet (549 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube Those were enough to make it accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 7.2 seconds. It may not sound like much now that pickup trucks come with supercar figures, but back in the day, it was remarkably quick, especially because the V8 had to push forward a vehicle that tipped the scales at 4,500 pounds (2,041 kilograms).
Top speed was electronically limited from the factory to 110 mph (161 kph). It was not only the electronic governor programmed by GM into the computer chip to cut fuel around that speed, but also the brick-like aerodynamics that limited it.
A custom-made can from New Era sits under the hood, hosting the expansion tank, the cooling tank, and the catch can. The stock 4L80E four-speed automatic transmission with a torque converter puts the power down through the rear wheels. The stock driveshaft and stock rear end, shortened with Dutchman axles, are part of the plan.
Diego and his friends rebuilt the suspension, installed new front and rear coilovers as part of a QA1 Stage 3 coilover conversion kit, firewall tubs, and drivetrain. Diego came up with jumper ports in the load bed for those 'just in case' moments. A Twisted MetalWorkz fuel tank replaced the original one.
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube The truck rides on Bogart wheels, measuring 20 x 9 inches with 265/40 20" tires up front and 21 x 11.5 inches with 315/30 20" rubber out back, while 16-inch Wilwood disc brakes with six-piston calipers at all four corners provide the stopping power.
The red fabric-wrapped seats on board the truck remind Shawn of Autotopia LA of grandma's couch. Diego wouldn’t change that for the world. Dakota Digital gauges indicate all the relevant driving data. They mimic the factory 1993 analog layout when the truck is off, but light up with modern digital readouts when fired up. The truck is missing the center console, but Diego will come up with one. The original one succumbed to age.
On the road, with Shawn in the driver’s seat and Diego, for the first time, in the passenger seat, the LS3-powered truck is the perfect cruiser, quiet and comfortable. When you step on it, it loses good manners, but remains super responsive and predictable. On launch, it spins the tires like no tomorrow, leaving a cloud of smoke as it drives off. Not many ICEs out there can keep up with it.

Forgotten 1966 Dodge Charger Is a Sad Sight, Nice Surprise Inside the Cabin
13 photos
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Josh Cox
When it comes to the classic Dodge Charger, most people seem to favor the 1968-1971 versions. And I get why: these cars look terrific and can be fast when fitted with big-block V8 engines. But I have a thing for the first-generation Charger . There's something about that fastback design and the "electric razor" grille.
The original Charger debuted in January 1966, and the company described it as the "leader of the Dodge rebellion." And indeed it was. Not only did it introduce the iconic 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Street Hemi, but it also looked unlike any other B-body Mopar. The fastback design, the upscale interior, and the four-seat layout gave it a unique position on the market.
But this recipe didn't catch on; customers were more interested in the more traditional muscle cars. The first-year Charger was relatively successful, with 37,344 units sold, but deliveries dropped to only 15,788 examples in 1967. As a result, Dodge gave the B-body a radical makeover for the 1968 model year.
Nearly 60 years later, the first-gen Charger is nowhere near as desirable as the post-1967 iterations. And surprisingly enough, you can still buy Hemi-equipped examples for under $100,000. As for the non-Hemi cars, most of them are basically doomed to become rust buckets. This 1966 fastback is one of those Chargers struggling for a second chance.
The Mopar surfaced in Cartersville, Georgia, and it looks like it's been sitting for a very long time. It was probably parked in this yard decades ago, losing much of its paint due to exposure to the elements. But it's not terrible when it comes to rust, and the interior is almost complete and surprisingly solid.
The seller says the vehicle is black, but the body panels show at least three different hues. There's blue paint on the driver-side rear fender and a cream color on the other side. There's some black as well, along with a large amount of surface rust.
There's no confirmation on whether the engine is numbers-matching , but the powerplant looks legit. It's a 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8, which is both good news and bad news. The good news is that it's not a totally undesirable small-block mill. On the other hand, the 383 is not as sought-after as the Hemi or 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB, either.
And it's not exactly rare. Dodge dropped the four-barrel 383 V8 into 12,328 cars, which is a third of the total 1966-model-year production. However, this Charger hides a nice surprise inside the cabin. It's a manual shifter, which makes this Mopar notably rarer. Specifically, only 2,809 vehicles were equipped with the 383 V8 and four-speed manual combo.
And while this figure is still somewhat big, it's worth considering that many of these cars are in far worse shape. This Charger may actually be worth saving. But is it also worth the $15,000 asking price ? Let me know in the comments section below.

Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 14, 2026
Canadian explorer Boron One Holdings (TSXV: BONE) has outlined a higher projected return, annual revenue and after-tax net present value (NPV) for its Piskanja boron project in Serbia.
An updated preliminary economic assessment (PEA) released Wednesday forecasts an after-tax internal rate of return of 89%, compared with 79% in the 2022 study. At a 10% discount rate, the NPV rises about 6% to $558.8 million (C$799 million) from $524.9 million, while average annual gross revenue increases to $140.4 million from $126 million.
Initial capital costs remain unchanged at $79.9 million, with payback projected within a year of starting commercial production. However, the proposed mine life falls to 13 years from 16, while average annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization drop to $87.7 million from $91.3 million.
The economic assessment excludes inferred resources. The study remains preliminary, and the resources don’t have demonstrated economic viability.
“Given these and other factors, future activities are justified to continue to advance project development,” Boron One said in Wednesday’s statement. A future work program will be discussed to define the necessary steps toward a feasibility study and the eventual construction of an underground mine, it added.
High-tech applications
Boron is considered a critical mineral in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union, but not in Canada. Its compounds are used in fertilizers, specialty glass, ceramics, fibreglass insulation, as well as electrolyte additives in some electric-vehicle batteries.
Turkey and the U.S. are the world’s largest boron producers, according to the U.S. Geological Survey . Turkey holds an estimated 950 million tonnes of reserves, expressed as boron trioxide content, by far the largest of any reporting country. Other significant producers include Bolivia, Chile, China and Peru.
Measured and indicated resources at Piskanja total 7.1 million tonnes grading 32.4% boron trioxide for 2.3 million contained tonnes of the compound, according to an estimate dated Oct. 12. The project is in southern Serbia, about 160 km south of Belgrade by road. A 2022 estimate outlined measured and indicated resources of 6.9 million tonnes grading 34.4% boron trioxide for 2.36 million contained tonnes.
Borate mineralization at Piskanja is hosted in sedimentary rocks. The deposit includes colemanite, ulexite and howlite, minerals used in products and industrial applications that rely on boron. Boron One has been advancing technical studies and pursuing the approvals needed to develop the project.
A binding offtake agreement signed in May covers at least 25,000 tonnes of boron products annually for three years from the start of operational production, with an option to increase purchases to 50,000 tonnes. The unnamed buyer’s commitment is subject to required permits and a successful plant qualification trial.
Different mix
The new study assumes prices of $650 per tonne for sales-grade colemanite and ulexite concentrates and $1,000 per tonne for technical-grade boric acid. Capital and operating cost estimates have an accuracy range of plus or minus 35%, the company said.
All-in sustaining costs are estimated at $231.44 per tonne of product, Boron One says. Sustaining capital over the mine life is forecast at $38.1 million.
The new PEA incorporates additional metallurgical and processing tests, a three-dimensional resource model distinguishing different borate types, revised mine designs, geotechnical testing, updated market studies and environmental work.
Boron One’s revised plan also changes the mix of products expected to be sold. Average annual commercial production is projected at 157,600 tonnes of colemanite and 83,800 tonnes of ulexite, two borate minerals, alongside 25,000 tonnes of boric acid. The 2022 study had forecast annual production of about 258,300 tonnes of sales-grade colemanite and 25,000 tonnes of boric acid.
Shares of Boron One last closed at 3¢ in Toronto, giving the company a market value of about C$9 million (US$6.3 million). The stock has traded between 2.5¢ and 9.5¢ in the past year.

Gold doré bar cools following a pour. Credit: Henry Lazenby
Posted By: Colin McClelland October 14, 2026
Gold producers aren’t getting full credit from investors for stronger profits and tighter spending discipline, Sprott Asset Management says.
The NYSE Arca Gold Miners Index traded at 5.7 times expected operating earnings at Sept. 30, about 22% below its roughly 7.3-times average over the past 20 years. Its forward earnings-per-share measure has climbed to more than four times its level at the end of 2023, according to the Toronto-based investment manager.
“We believe that major gold miners favour capital discipline and profitability, which has at least been partly reflected in their balance sheets and rising shareholder distributions,” Director of Research & Investment Strategy Kenny Zhu said in an emailed reply to The Northern Miner . “Net debt levels have fallen to their lowest point in the past 20 years, even as return on capital rises and shareholder distributions increase.”
The disconnect tests whether producers have broken the spending habits that disappointed shareholders after the 2011 gold boom. Stronger finances support Sprott’s argument, but pressure to replace depleted deposits could require more construction spending and acquisitions, potentially testing that discipline.
Valuation gap
The index’s forward enterprise-value-to-EBITDA multiple stood at 6.59 times at the end of 2023, Zhu said. The measure compares the value of a business, including debt and subtracting cash, with expected earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.
The discount to the long-term average doesn’t alone establish that miners are cheap, he acknowledged. Sprott’s argument is that valuations may understate earnings forecasts that remain near historical highs.
The index’s 12-month forward earnings-per-share measure rose about 4.4 times between the end of 2023 and Sept. 30, according to Sprott’s quarterly report , published Oct. 7. Those figures represent expected earnings rather than profits already earned.
Investors may instead be anticipating lower gold prices, Zhu said. Higher costs and operational setbacks could also erode miners’ margins.
Gold producers remain overlooked despite stronger finances, Toronto-based investment dealer Maison Placements Canada President John Ing wrote in his September report, Gold: An October Reckoning?
“Gold miners have become value plays,” veteran gold analyst Ing wrote. “Most have rock solid balance sheets, churning out record cash flows and will end the year with record dividend payments.”
Cash cushion
BMO Capital Markets’ latest GoldPages report supplies company-level evidence of those stronger finances. Cash held by its producer universe exceeded debt by about $19.6 billion (C$28 billion), based on the latest reported quarterly balance sheets, mostly from June.
Agnico Eagle Mines (TSX, NYSE: AEM) had about $3.3 billion in net cash, while Barrick Mining (TSX: ABX; NYSE: B) had about $1.2 billion, BMO’s Oct. 12 report showed. Net cash means cash on the balance sheet exceeds short- and long-term debt.
Their valuations nevertheless differ. Using BMO’s commodity-price forecasts and Oct. 9 share prices, Agnico traded at 7.3 times forecast 2026 EBITDA, compared with 3.5 times for Barrick.
Those company estimates aren’t directly comparable with Sprott’s rolling 12-month index measure. They illustrate how differently investors value producers within the same sector.
Ing favours Agnico’s growth prospects and Barrick’s asset portfolio, but cautions that strong finances don’t eliminate the need to replenish production.
“Reserve replacement is key but few miners have been successful, suggesting continued M&A activity,” he wrote.
Growth test
BMO’s forecasts show that growth prospects vary considerably. Agnico’s gold-equivalent production is forecast to fall about 3% next year to 3.2 million oz., while Barrick’s is expected to rise about 13% to 4.3 million ounces. The measure includes other metals converted into equivalent gold ounces.
Ing also points to producers taking stakes in explorers as a way to build future growth options. Agnico’s Radisson investment , announced in August, supports underground exploration at the O’Brien gold project in Quebec.
The balance between replacing reserves and avoiding excessive spending is also a concern for Sprott Managing Partner John Hathaway, who urged producers to put reserve replacement first and avoid diluting shareholders in an interview with The Northern Miner last month.
Sprott’s investment case also depends on gold retaining support from reserve diversification and central bank demand. Ing maintains an interim bullion target of $6,000 per oz., citing U.S. fiscal deficits and geopolitical uncertainty.
Central bank demand remains substantial but uneven. Net purchases totalled 345 tonnes in the first half, the lowest first-half total since 2022, despite a sharp second-quarter rebound, the World Gold Council said in its July report .
For miners, the question is whether stronger earnings and balance sheets will survive both bullion-price volatility and the investment needed to sustain production. Zhu argues the evidence doesn’t yet suggest a broad return to excessive risk-taking.
“Although the conditions for risk-taking may return, we believe management teams would likely need to pursue aggressive M&A, substantially ramp up their exploration activity, and pay significant valuation premiums for acquisitions,” he said. “Generally, the data do not currently suggest that has occurred.”

Revolution Medicines’ recently approved drug showed a 24% overall response rate and a high rate of side effects in patients whose cancer has a G12D mutation, reinforcing Mizuho’s view that a more specific agent such as Verastem Oncology’s VS-7375 “should come first for G12D patients.”
Less than a week after detailed subgroup data from Revolution Medicines’ newly approved pancreatic cancer drug shook the biotech’s stock, Verastem Oncology has shown “robust clinical activity” in one of those very subgroups.
In the Phase 1/2 TARGET-D 101 trial , Verastem’s oral KRAS G12D–targeting inhibitor VS-7375 showed “robust clinical activity with a favorable safety and tolerability profile” across multiple dose levels and tumor types, the biotech reported Wednesday. The study, which has enrolled 295 patients, was designed to assess the safety and efficacy of VS-7375 alone and in combination for patients with advanced solid tumors harboring a KRAS G12D mutation, including pancreatic, colorectal and non-small cell lung cancers.
Half of patients, or four of eight with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (mPDAC) who received 900 mg of VS-7375 daily in the second-line setting, saw a confirmed objective response rate (ORR) after an average of 6.4 months, Verastem said. In 14 patients treated in third- and fourth-line settings, the confirmed ORR was 36%.
The pancreatic cancer data are particularly notable after the FDA released review documents last week showing that RevMed’s recently approved RAS inhibitor Rasonque was more effective in some mutation subgroups than others. While the drug reached a 33% ORR across all KRAS mutations in the Phase 3 RASolute 302 trial, the response was not equal in all patients. Half of those whose cancer possesses a G12V mutation saw a response. But the ORR in patients with a G12D mutation—who represented 43% of the trial—was 24%, and just 7% of participants with G12R mutations responded.

RevMed’s Rasonque gets a subtype data asterisk, but analysts remain bullish
Data released by the FDA show that Revolution Medicine’s newly approved pancreatic cancer drug underperformed in a large subgroup of patients, but analysts say the biotech still has a clear winner.
October 12, 2026
·
2 min read

Michael Gibney
Read more
Verastem’s PDAC results met the expectations of Mizuho analysts, who had been looking for a confirmed ORR for VS-7375 of 35% or greater in these patients.
With Rasonque showing a confirmed ORR of just 24% in patients with KRAS G12D mutations--along with skin and gastrointestinal adverse events and required dose reductions, “this reinforces our view that an allele-specific agent should come first for G12D patients, with pan-RAS reserved for later lines or combinations,” the analysts wrote.
VS-7375 is a selective oral KRAS G12D dual ON/OFF inhibitor—meaning it is designed to bind both the active and inactive states of the mutated protein.
Across Verastem’s TARGET-D trial, 2% of patients discontinued treatment due to adverse events, with the most common treatment-related adverse events (TRAE) at a 900-mg dose being low-grade nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Serious TRAEs occurred in 10% of patients, with 2% seeing serious GI TRAEs. There were two deaths in the modified intent-to-treat population, but both were unrelated to treatment with VS-7375, Verastem said.
With these results, Verastem will move VS-7375 into a Phase 3 trial in first-line mPDAC, the design of which the FDA has signed off on, the company said Wednesday. That trial is set to kick off by the end of this year.
Meanwhile, Verastem’s candidate also met or came close to meeting Mizuho’s expectations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer (CRC), where the analysts were hoping to see ORRs of at least 50% and 30%, respectively.
Patients with NSCLC treated in the second-line setting or later with 600 mg of VS-7375 experienced a 43% confirmed ORR. “Durable responses were observed and PFS is trending favorably,” Verastem reported. As for CRC—for which the drug was being tested in the third-line setting—900 mg of VS-7375 combined with anti-EGFR therapy led to 33% unconfirmed ORR.
KRAS G12D mutations account for just over a quarter of all KRAS mutations and are most prevalent in pancreatic and colorectal cancers at 40% and 15%, respectively, according to Verastem’s Wednesday release. There are currently no FDA-approved therapies specifically targeting this mutation in cancer.
“Patients with KRAS G12D-driven cancers deserve an effective, highly targeted therapy suitable for long-term treatment,” Michael Kauffman, president of development at Verastem, said in a prepared statement. “Today’s first multi-tumor clinical dataset for VS-7375 demonstrates compelling and robust responses across KRAS G12D-mutated cancers, marking an important development milestone and reinforcing our conviction that VS-7375 has the potential to become both a best-in-class therapy and the first therapy used for these patients.”

Car Guy Got 1969 Charger R/T Hemi 4-Speed After Watching Bullitt in 1975, He Loves Driving It Still
67 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Dodge made three grand debuts for the legendary Charger: once in 1966, on January 1, the second time on September 14, 1967, and the third on October 17, 1968. The first time was the absolute premiere for the moniker, the second saw the introduction of the revered second generation, and the third was the first public screening of “Bullitt.”
Say what you will, but those ten minutes and fifty-three seconds it starred alongside Steve McQueen were the best advertising spot the Charger enjoyed before or since. You need proof of that? Typical shelf life of a TV spot in the late sixties hovered between six months to a year. “Bullitt” kept the Charger evergreen to 2026, but as far as its commercial success went, the movie sold a second-gen Charger a full nineteen years after its debut.
In 1975, Bob Dyrda was a college senior, and dreamt about muscle ccars. Fatefully, he watched a television rerun of the classic blockbuster “Bullitt,” and he enthusiastically noted, "I settled on the Charger and that was all it took." For the following twelve years, he diligently saved his penny and he saved his dime, for he knew there would be a time when he would buy a brand-new 426.
Sorry for not going through with the Beach Boys theme song, but Bob’s Charger couldn’t have come with the legendary Chevy big-block. Instead, the gearhead had to settle for a Chrysler offer, so he got an old drag racer second-gen Dodge Charger with a big ol’ orange engine under the hood. One that matched its name with the sobriquet of the paint used on that very block. 426 Hemi, in Hemi Orange.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Yup. The man has a Hemi Charger. Need I say more? How about a pair of 4s? 4-speed, 4.10 Dana 60. And 46,006 miles. Or, to be accurate, that’s how many it had in late June 2026, when Lou Costabile asked the owner out for a shootout. For YouTube. The result is embedded below.
The owner is probably a strong manifester, because he bought an original 1969 Dodge Charger brochure before acquiring his actual unicorn. Yes, Bullitt’s bad guys rode in a ’68 R/T, but Bob liked the taillight of the ’69 better. THE TAILLIGHTS! The man is clearly a strong-willed gearhead with non-mainstream tastes. Everyone is head over (w)heels with the signature round lamps of the ’68, and he casually says “No, thanks. I’ll take the better-looking ones.”
The ’69 is clearly a fan’s favorite for the signature feature found at the opposite end of the back lights – namely, the split grille that made TV screen waves in the Dukes of Hazzard series. To each their own. Besides, Bob doesn’t really get to see how he looks like driving his 4-speeed Hemi Charger from the outside, mainly because he’s in the car – and loving every nanosecond of it.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile So, after he got the original brochure and patiently waited to turn his ultimate high-octane dream into a fantastic reality, Bob found the perfect car. The story took a romantic turn in 1987 while discussing marriage with his future girlfriend Maryanne.
She supported his automotive passion, wisely advising, "Well if you really want this car why don't you get it before we get married otherwise life will probably take us away from it." Bob placed an ad in Hemmings Motor News, eventually flying out to New York to buy this modified drag racer for 8,500 dollars.
The dream-come-true new owner struck gold by finding two original factory broadcast sheets and the fender tag, confirming the car is a true “Y14” Sold Car ordered strictly for racing. Built with a 426 Hemi engine and a 4-speed manual transmission with a Hurst shifter, it features the A34 Super Track Pak. In Dodge parlance, that’s the Dana 60 rear axle with 4.10 gears, a 26-inch radiator, and power front disc brakes.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Stripped of extra weight, the car was ordered as a radio-delete model, featuring only a remote driver mirror and a locking gas cap as options. Bob purchased this brute in 1987 from Dave Schwarz in Massapequa, New York, who had bought it in 1986 from a man named Ed in Bay Shore. A handwritten sheet passed down from owner to owner also mysteriously mentioned a connection with a certain Joe Garity. You’ll understand the reason and rhyme behind this list of random names if you watch the video.
Because the engine underwent extensive modifications at Bob Sharp Racing in Danbury, Connecticut, Bob Dyrda suspects the car originally lived there. Supporting this theory, he discovered a vintage Connecticut license plate reading hidden underneath the back seat cushion. A July 1971 renewal sticker completely covered a previous 1970 sticker, strongly suggesting the vehicle belonged to a Connecticut resident from 1969 until it was likely sold to a second owner around 1971.
The handwritten notes detailed a serious high-performance engine rebuild. The already unhinged (but hotter than the hot hinges of you-know-what) motor was balanced, blueprinted, ported, and polished, receiving new 12.5:1 compression pistons, a Crower camshaft, and upgraded valvetrain components.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The original Carter carburetors were swapped for a pair of Carter Competition 750 CFM carburetors, while the factory dual-breaker distributor was replaced by a Mallory electronic ignition system and high-performance spark plug wires to extract every drop of performance from the power stroke.
Serious racers spare no expense, and this vehicle received Hooker headers to replace the cast iron exhaust manifolds. A separate Ford starter solenoid was installed on the inner fender to accommodate those massive headers. Furthermore, the 4-speed transmission was significantly beefed-up using Fairbanks performance components.
When Bob bought the car, it wore unidentified aftermarket wheels, but the previous owner kept them, allowing selling the car to Bob with standard Chrysler stamped steelies.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The exterior wore a fresh coat of factory-correct red paint, but the iconic white R/T tail stripe had been removed, leaving only faint remnants under the trunk lid. To save the last ounce of weight and morph this muscle car into a sleeper, previous owners removed both door emblems and the front bumper guards.
In the engine bay, a misaligned driver hood hinge caused a stress crack in the subframe, which was later repaired with a small welded metal patch. Inside the cabin, the front seat headrests were removed, and the factory wood-grained shifter knob was replaced by a Hurst T-handle. Although originally a radio-delete car, someone added a Chrysler AM radio featuring a 1968 faceplate, routing it to a broken fender antenna.
Scratches on the steering column suggest an aftermarket tachometer was previously mounted there. Under the hood, an incorrect power drum brake master cylinder had replaced the original unit. In the 39 years since he’s owned it (bought in October, 1987), Bob Dyrda took the car back to as close to factory as possible, and today he prides himself in driving one of the best-looking Hemi Chargers of the second-gen era. He even built a website for it , specifically to find out more of its history.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The Charger R/T moniker debuted in 1968, with Dodge building 475 Hemi cars. This limited production run consisted of 211 units equipped with 4-speed manual transmissions, while the remaining 264 vehicles received the heavy-duty three-speed automatic gearboxes.
For the legendary 1969 model year, Dodge assembled 432 Charger R/T Hemis. Out of those, 207 examples featured the highly desirable 4-speed manual transmission, and 225 came with automatics. By 1970, soaring insurance premiums effectively killed the muscle car market, causing production to plummet dramatically. Only 112 buyers stepped up for the ultimate engine option that year, perfectly split between 56 manual cars and 56 automatic vehicles.
The legendary big-block engine made its final appearance in 1971, with only 63 Charger R/Ts leaving the assembly line. That final batch included 30 manual transmission cars and 33 automatics. Across those 4 glorious production years, Dodge manufactured a grand total of just 1,082 Charger R/T Hemi vehicles.
Looking at the broader picture, the factory produced 53,195 Dodge Charger R/T models across all engine options during that memorable era, with the peak coming right in 1969, at 19,298 cars. All in all, the Charger R/T Hemi saw a grand total of 1,173 cars made between 1968 and 1971, of which 498 had three pedals and a big iron stick in the middle of the floor pan between the front passengers.

DP World has appointed Morten Johansen as chief executive officer of its Americas region, placing a longtime ports and logistics executive in charge of the company’s operations across North America, South America, and the Caribbean.
Johansen made the announcement in a LinkedIn post Oct. 13. He succeeds Brian Enright, who served in the dual positions since Oct. 22.
Johansen has more than 25 years of experience in integrated port and logistics businesses. He joined Dubai-based DP World in 2011 and previously served as CEO of DP World Dominicana.
He later became chief operating officer of DP World Americas, with responsibility for ports and terminals, logistics services, economic zones, and maritime operations throughout the Western Hemisphere.
In that role, he has emphasized integrating physical infrastructure with ports, inland transport, customs processes, economic zones, and digital platforms.
The appointment comes as DP World continues to expand its Americas footprint.
The company entered exclusive negotiations with the Port of Corpus Christi in June 2026 to design, build, and operate a container terminal under a long-term lease. If completed, it would be DP World’s first container-terminal development on the U.S. Gulf Coast and its first U.S. container-terminal development in roughly two decades.
The proposed facility could ultimately handle about 1 million TEUs annually. No construction start date, final capital commitment, or definitive lease terms have been announced.
Other Americas initiatives include a $760 million port and free-trade-zone development in the Dominican Republic , which the company says is intended to increase cargo capacity and support nearshoring-related investment.
Prior to DP World, Johansen’s background includes senior roles at APM Terminals, Maersk, and Sociedade Gestora de Terminais. A native of Denmark, he has been based in Charlotte, N.C., in his Americas leadership role.
